parole.testo: This vessel is considered classically an Indian vessel; so it is likely connected to Sanskrit बेड (beḍa), Hindi बेड़ा (beṛā, “boat”).

From various descendants of Sanskrit जम्बुल (jambula). The most common form, here chosen as the title, is apparently thus extremely garbled by Egyptian Arabic speakers owing to the plant, requiring intense tropical conditions, growing only at scattered spots of the Arabic-speaking countries – limite

parole.significato: a collective term for the brahmin caste
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Sanskrit ब्राह्मण (brā́hmaṇa). In a pseudo-etymology by Muslim scholars, it was said to come from the same root as إِبْرَاهِيم (ʔibrāhīm, “Abraham”) in order to indicate an Abrahamic origin for Vedantic monotheism/monism and to categorise Hindus as People of the Book.

parole.significato: the betel pepper and the betel leaf – as opposed to the betel nut فَوْفَل (fawfal)
parole.testo: From Sanskrit ताम्बूल (tāmbūla). The form تَانَبُول (tānabūl) is a learned borrowing from Persian تانبول (tânbul), the form تَامُول (tāmūl) an unlearned adaptation towards a triliteral of it or another Indian descendant of the Sanskrit.
Borrowed from Sanskrit जीव (jīva, “sine, chord, life, existence”).

parole.significato: teak tree and wood (Tectona gen. et spp.)
parole.testo: Compare Aramaic שָׁאגָא / שָׁגָא / ܫܓܐ (šāgā), Persian ساج (sâj). Ultimately from Sanskrit शाक (śāka, “vegetable; herb; teak-tree”); compare vernacular Hindi सागौन (sāgaun, “teak-tree”) and Bengali সেগুন (śegun, “teak-tree”) for the consonantism.

parole.significato: offspring of a sheep or (more widely) a goat; lamb or kid
parole.testo: As in some Bedouin dialects also with the first consonant emphatic (صَحَل (ṣaḥal), maybe from Sanskrit छागल (chāgala), छाग (chāga, “goat”), but in an original meaning of a newborn kid, with the meanings of “imperfect” dates or anything imperfect transferred, and from the brutal process of birth a de
Through a modern Indian language from Sanskrit शिरीष (śirīṣa), which actually means Albizia lebbeck known as لَبَخ (labaḵ).
Semantic loan from Sanskrit शू॒न्य (śūnyá, “zero”, literally “empty; void”). Compare صَفْر (ṣafr, “empty; void”, with variant صِفْر (ṣifr)).

parole.significato: baobarang, false black pepper (Embelia ribes; also Embelia tsjeriam-cottam syn. Embelia robusta)
parole.testo: More direct borrowing of Sanskrit विडङ्ग (viḍaṅga), विडङ्गा (viḍaṅgā), which has also been borrowed via Persian برنگ (berang) as بِرَنْج (biranj).

parole.significato: aloeswood and in particular its seeds
parole.testo: Corruption of Sanskrit कालागुरु (kālāguru, “a kind of black aloe”) and perhaps another word with काल (kāla, “a kind of black aloe”) other than with अगरु (agaru, “aloe”).

parole.significato: Curcuma and especially Curcuma longa, turmeric, Indian saffron
parole.testo: Semitic cognates include Aramaic כּוּרְכְּמָא, ܟܽܘܪܟܡܳܐ (kurkmā), Akkadian 𒌑𒆪𒄀𒆸𒈾 (/⁠kurkanū⁠/), Hebrew כַּרְכֹּם / כַּרְכֹּום (karkom); however because of non-philological evidence it is a preferred assumption that the Arabic word comes via India, from Sanskrit कुङ्कुम (kuṅkuma). Since the expansion of Arabic into South Arabia and the Iraq, ultimately from Sanskrit हरिद्रा (haridrā), with vocalism change in Arabic as in قُطُب (quṭub), وُرُس (wurus) etc.
